steps.name: Build the number
steps.narration: Each card is a place. Drop digits in to build 3040.507: 3 thousands, 4 tens, 5 tenths and 7 thousandths.
steps.prompt: Which card does the 4 go in?

steps.name: Worth
steps.narration: The worth line shows what each digit is really worth. The 3 is worth 3000, but the 7 is only worth 0.007.

steps.name: Placeholder zeros
steps.narration: The zeros in hundreds, ones and hundredths hold the places open. Without them the 3 would slide down to a smaller place.
steps.prompt: Why do we need the 0 in the hundreds?

steps.name: Multiply by 10
steps.narration: 23.6 times 10: every digit glides one card to the left. The decimal point stays still. 23.6 becomes 236.

steps.name: Placeholder drops in
steps.narration: 4.7 times 100: the digits glide two cards left to make 470. The ones card is now empty, so a gold zero drops in to hold the place.

steps.name: Divide by 100
steps.narration: 61.5 divided by 100: two cards to the right. A zero drops into the ones card: 0.615.
steps.prompt: What goes in the ones card?

steps.name: Counters
steps.narration: Each counter is worth its column. 2 hundreds, 4 tens and 3 ones make 243.

steps.name: Decimal columns
steps.narration: Right of the decimal point, counters are worth 0.1 and 0.01. 1 one, 3 tenths and 6 hundredths make 1.36.
steps.prompt: What is a counter in the tenths column worth?

steps.name: Too many!
steps.narration: Add 0.48: 4 more tenths and 8 more hundredths. The hundredths column now has 14 counters. It glows: time to exchange!

steps.name: Exchange
steps.narration: Ten hundredths gather, merge with a flash into one tenth, and fly to the tenths column. 1.36 plus 0.48 is 1.84.

steps.name: Break one
steps.narration: To take 1.5 from 3.2, break one of the ones into 10 tenths. They fan out: 2 ones and 12 tenths, still 3.2.
steps.prompt: Is the value the same after breaking?

steps.name: Blocks
steps.narration: A unit is 1, a rod is 10 units, a flat is 100. 2 flats, 3 rods and 5 units make 235.
steps.prompt: How many units make a rod?

steps.name: Build a ten
steps.narration: There are 12 units: too many! Ten units slide together and snap into one rod, then the rod joins the tens.

steps.name: Fuse a hundred
steps.narration: 13 rods: ten rods slide side by side and fuse into a flat. 1 hundred becomes 2 hundreds.
steps.prompt: How many rods make a flat?

steps.name: Break to subtract
steps.narration: 204 has no tens. Break a flat: it splits into 10 rods. Now 1 flat, 10 rods and 4 units: still 204.

steps.name: Decimal blocks
steps.narration: Change what the flat is worth. If a flat is 1, a rod is 0.1 and a unit is 0.01. This shows 1.36.
steps.prompt: What is a rod worth now?

steps.name: Partition
steps.narration: 23 × 14: split each number by place value. 23 is 20 + 3, 14 is 10 + 4. The grid has a cell for each pair.

steps.name: Add the parts
steps.prompt: Why do we add the parts?

steps.name: Short division
steps.narration: 756 ÷ 3: 7 ÷ 3 = 2 remainder 1. The 1 hundred becomes 10 tens and flies across: 15 tens ÷ 3 = 5. Then 6 ÷ 3 = 2. Answer 252.

steps.name: Decimal remainder
steps.narration: 7 ÷ 4 = 1 remainder 3. Put in a decimal point and placeholder zeros: 30 tenths ÷ 4 = 7 r 2, 20 hundredths ÷ 4 = 5. 7 ÷ 4 = 1.75.

steps.name: Big numbers
steps.narration: 30 700 in standard form is 3.07 × 10⁴: a number from 1 to under 10, times a power of ten. The gold digit sits in the 10⁴ place.

steps.name: Count the hops
steps.narration: 45 000: hop the decimal point left until only one non-zero digit is in front of it. Four hops, so 45 000 = 4.5 × 10⁴.

steps.name: Small numbers
steps.narration: 0.00062: now the point hops right, four times. Hopping right gives a negative power: 6.2 × 10⁻⁴.

steps.name: Scale the power
steps.narration: Slide the power from 4 to 6 on the number line: every digit glides two places left. 3.07 × 10⁶ = 3 070 000.
steps.prompt: What does +2 on the power do?

steps.name: Compare
steps.narration: Compare 3.2 × 10⁵ (A) and 9.1 × 10⁴ (B): check the powers first. 10⁵ is bigger, so A is bigger, even though 9.1 > 3.2.

steps.name: Square numbers
steps.narration: Drag the corner to grow a square. A 5 by 5 square has 25 tiles: 5² = 25.
steps.prompt: How many tiles in a 5 by 5 square?

steps.name: Square root
steps.narration: The square root undoes squaring. Which square has 49 tiles? Grow it until it matches: 7 × 7 = 49, so √49 = 7.

steps.name: Cube numbers
steps.narration: A cube 3 by 3 by 3 is built from 27 small cubes: 3³ = 27.

steps.name: Index notation
steps.narration: Repeated multiplication: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2. Four factors of 2 is written 2⁴, which is 16.

steps.name: Multiply powers
steps.narration: 2³ × 2²: the two chains join into one chain of 5 twos. Add the indices: 2⁵.

steps.name: Divide powers
steps.narration: 3⁵ ÷ 3²: each 3 on the bottom cancels a 3 on top. Three 3s are left: 3³. Subtract the indices.

steps.name: Fractional index
steps.narration: 8 to the power one third means the cube root of 8: the edge of a cube with volume 8. The edge is 2.

steps.name: The tree
steps.narration: 3 + 4 × 2 as a tree. The operation lowest in the tree is done first. × sits below +, so 4 × 2 comes first.

steps.name: Collapse
steps.narration: The branches 4 and 2 slide up into ×, which becomes 8. Then 3 and 8 collapse into + to give 11.

steps.name: Brackets first
steps.narration: (3 + 4) × 2: the brackets push + down the tree, so it is worked out first. 7 × 2 = 14.

steps.name: Powers
steps.narration: 2 + 3² × 4: the power is lowest of all, then ×, then +. 3² = 9, 9 × 4 = 36, 2 + 36 = 38.

steps.name: Left to right
steps.narration: 12 ÷ 3 × 2: ÷ and × have equal priority, so work left to right. 12 ÷ 3 = 4, then 4 × 2 = 8 (not 12 ÷ 6).

steps.name: Put it together
steps.narration: 10 − 2 × (1 + 3) + 6: brackets 4, then 2 × 4 = 8, then left to right: 10 − 8 = 2, 2 + 6 = 8.

steps.name: Place
steps.narration: Each + counter is worth +1, each − counter is worth −1. Four + counters make 4: the marker sits at 4.

steps.name: Add negatives
steps.narration: 4 + (−6): drop six − counters onto the mat. Pairs of + and − are zero pairs.

steps.name: Cross zero
steps.narration: Cancel the zero pairs: four pairs vanish, two − counters are left. The marker has crossed zero to −2.

steps.name: Make room
steps.narration: 2 − 5: there are only two + counters to take away. Add three zero pairs (worth 0), then take away five +. Three − are left: −3.
steps.prompt: Do zero pairs change the value?

steps.name: Value reading
steps.narration: −3 − (−4): take away four − counters. Add one zero pair first, then take four − away: 1 is left.

sub.label: 2 − 5: add zero pairs, then take away

steps.name: Fill the frame
steps.narration: A ten frame holds 10. Drop in 7 counters, one per cell, five in each row.

steps.name: Split into a bond
steps.narration: The whole is 10. The 7 counters are one part. The other part is the empty cells.

steps.name: Partner glows
steps.narration: The three empty cells glow: 3 is the partner of 7. 7 + 3 = 10.

steps.name: Bonds to 20
steps.narration: Two frames make 20. 13 counters leave 7 empty cells: 13 + 7 = 20.

steps.name: Bonds to 1
steps.narration: Now each counter is 0.1. Six counters make 0.6; four tenths are empty, so 0.6 + 0.4 = 1.

steps.name: Bonds to 100
steps.narration: Each counter is 10. Seven make 70; three empty cells are 30: 70 + 30 = 100. Same pattern as 7 + 3 = 10.

steps.name: The square
steps.narration: The hundred square: each row is a ten. Moving right adds 1; moving down a row adds 10. The marker is on 23.

steps.name: Move by tens
steps.narration: +10: the marker drops one row, straight down. 23 + 10 = 33. The ones digit stays the same.
steps.prompt: Why does the ones digit stay 3?

steps.name: Tens and ones
steps.narration: +9 is +10 then −1: down one row, back one cell. 33 + 9 = 42.

steps.name: Land
steps.narration: +11 is +10 then +1: down and right. 42 + 11 = 53.

steps.name: Multiples
steps.narration: Multiples of 4 light up: 4, 8, 12, … They make columns that shift: every multiple of 4 is even.

steps.name: Pattern of 9
steps.narration: Multiples of 9 run in a diagonal: each step is +10 −1. The digits always add to 9.
steps.prompt: What is the next multiple of 9 after 45?

steps.name: Factors
steps.narration: Factors of 24 glow gold: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. Factors divide 24 exactly; multiples are 24, 48, 72, 96.

steps.name: Choose base
steps.narration: In base 10 the places are powers of 10: 1000, 100, 10, 1, and each place holds 0 to 9. 207 is 2 hundreds, 0 tens, 7 ones.
steps.prompt: What is the biggest digit in base 10?

steps.name: Fill places
steps.narration: Base 2 (binary): the places are powers of 2: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Each place is just on or off. Light 8, 2 and 1.

steps.name: Convert to denary
steps.narration: Add the place values that are on: 8 + 2 + 1 = 11. So 1011 in binary is 11 in denary.

steps.name: Carry
steps.narration: 0111 + 1: the ones place is full, so it carries. Each full place empties and passes 1 along: 1000, which is 8.

steps.name: Other bases
steps.narration: Base 5: places 125, 25, 5, 1 and digits 0 to 4. 324 in base 5 is 3 × 25 + 2 × 5 + 4 = 89.
steps.prompt: Why is there no digit 5 in base 5?

steps.name: Rings draw
steps.narration: The real numbers hold everything. Inside: rational numbers, then integers, then natural numbers. Irrational numbers sit in the reals but outside the rationals.

steps.name: Natural numbers
steps.narration: 7 is a counting number. √9 = 3, so it is natural too. They go in the smallest ring, ℕ.

steps.name: Integers
steps.narration: −3 and 0 are whole numbers but not counting numbers, so their smallest set is ℤ.

steps.name: Rationals
steps.narration: 0.75 and 0.333… can be written as fractions of integers (three quarters, one third), so they are rational but not integers.

steps.name: Irrationals glow
steps.narration: √2 and π never end and never repeat. They cannot be written as a fraction: they are irrational.

steps.name: All real
steps.narration: Every card sits inside ℝ. Each number goes in the smallest set it fits; it also belongs to every set around it.
